newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS-Buba to revalue reserves for Bonn's EMU bid.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Buba to revalue reserves for Bonn's EMU bid.

text.p: The German government and the fiercely independent Bundesbank agreed on Thursday to revalue the central bank's currency reserves this year to give a boost to Bonn's bid to join European monetary union.

Finance Minister Theo Waigel and Bundesbank President Hans Tietmeyer hammered out the final details of the plan, which could provide the government with well over 10 billion marks ($5.8 billion) in additional revenue that it will use to pay off old debt.

The plan was first hinted at last month when Waigel stunned financial markets with a scheme to change Bundesbank law and force it to revalue its huge gold and currency reserves to improve Bonn's chances of qualifying for monetary union.
The move prompted criticism that Bonn was seeking to use the same kind of creative accounting to qualify for monetary union that it so vehemently forbid other EU members to do.

The Bundesbank reacted angrily to the plan, seeing it as an attack on its independence and a bad precedent for Germany to set as European Union members are all scrambling to meet the targets for economic and monetary union (EMU).

The deal that was finally revealed after a lengthy meeting between Waigel and Tietmeyer on Thursday afternoon reflects a compromise that allows Bonn to benefit from revaluation of foreign exchange reserves but appears to leave its gold untouched until after the start of EMU.
Waigel and Tietmeyer, laughing on the doorstep of the finance ministry as they announced the compromise, appeared satisfied with the agreement.
"We have not only found a solution but I think it is a good and sturdy solution," Tietmeyer told reporters.
The government and the Bundesbank outlined the main points of their agreement in a joint statement.

With the start of monetary union in 1999, the future European Central Bank will begin to take over monetary policy authority now exercised by the central banks of European Union member states, requiring changes in each bank's accounts.
During the transition, Bundesbank capital will be increased substantially and its accounting rules will be remodelled, allowing it to adapt to the practices of the European bank.

"The Bundesbank intends to make use of this possibility," the statement said, adding that it would use leeway provided by existing law to revalue its foreign exchange reserves this year at a higher level.
"These allow an evaluation of the currency reserves closer to the market, while maintaining the principle of lowest value," the statement said.

In order to guard against price fluctuations, the Bundesbank traditionally books its reserves at a rate well below going market rates. By revaluing the reserves closer to market rates, the Bundesbank will realise huge profits.

The central bank dismissed statements by sources in the Bonn coalition government who had said that Waigel and Tietmeyer agreed the Bundesbank would revalue its currency reserves at a rate of at least 1.50 marks. The current market rate is around 1.7250 marks.

The Bundesbank's currency reserves of $65.7 billion are thought to consist only of dollars and are currently booked at 1.3620 marks. Bonn coalition sources said this meant the central bank would transfer up to 13 billion marks to the government next year.
"No figures on the outcome of a revaluation were decided on, nor is it possible at present to define a figure," the central bank said in response to the sources' comments.

While the deal was not unexpected, independent economists were not certain whether it would actually have much impact on Bonn's efforts to bring its deficits within the limits spelled out in the Maastricht Treaty on monetary union.

"It is true that 1997 is the basis for the choice of which nations will enter European monetary union but one should take note that nations' budget plans for 1998 will also be taken into account," said Hermann Remsperger, chief economist at BHF-Bank in Frankfurt.
The deal had little impact on markets.

"I think it was clear that there would be an agreement. Both sides had signalled that this would be so," said Gerhard Grebe, chief economist at Bank Julius Baer in Frankfurt. -- william.boston@reuters.com (Bonn Newsroom, 49 228 26097 150) ($ = 1.731 German Marks)
